entries.outreach_draft:
Dear Sir Alfred Gilbert,

We are writing on behalf of the production 'Piccadilly Circus' to request permission to feature the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain (1893) in our film.

The Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain appears from 0:00:00 to 0:01:00 in the sample excerpt. The famous winged statue, commonly known as Eros, and its fountain base are centrally framed for the first part of the clip, and remain visible throughout.

We are seeking worldwide rights, for all media, in perpetuity.

The historical record documents County Council involvement, acceptance/arrangements, and expenditure, but does not identify the instrument or date transferring title or the successor/current physical custodian. We request guidance on the current owner or site manager for the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain. No separate U.S. copyright notice, registration, or first-publication record for this fountain was located. We would appreciate any information you can provide regarding its copyright status, particularly concerning U.S. publication.

Please confirm if you are able to grant this permission, advise on any associated fees, and inform us of any restrictions that may apply. We also request an artwork reproduction release.

citations.title: The Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain | British History Online
excerpts: The Council had not authorized this expenditure—the memorial was not yet the Council's property—and it was only after acrimonious correspondence that the matter was smoothed down by the secretary of the Memorial Committee, who finally persuaded the Council to pay. (fn. 46) By the summer of 1893 the memorial was at last ready to be unveiled, the castings having been made at the foundry of George Broad and Son. A large tent was erected nearby ('the restricted space was very fully occupied', commented _The Times_ ), and on 29 June the Duke of Westminster presided over a distinguished company, from which Gilbert himself was conspicuously absent. The honorary secretary read the report of the Memorial Committee, and the Duke, on behalf of the inhabitants of London, asked the chairman of the County Council to accept the monument. He 'then unveiled the fountain, and the Duchess of Westminster set the fountains in motion and, amid cheers drank the first cup of water from them'. Other speakers included Sir Harry Verney, who was aged ninety-one and had been at school at Harrow with Shaftesbury; he said 'I think this fountain is remarkably well designed, and it is a remarkably suitable memorial to Lord Shaftesbury, for it is always giving water to rich and poor alike at all times of day and night.' (fn. 47) At its unveiling the aspect of the memorial was not as it is now (Plate 154a).

excerpts: (fn. 19) Unfortunately the chains to which this passage appears to allude have long since been removed or stolen, but it was probably to this idea that Sir David Murray, R.A., referred when in 1930 he stated that Gilbert had 'had a pretty and delicate idea, which he skilfully carried out, of making every part of the memorial form the letter S, but where it was placed that had been unnoticed'. (fn. 71) After the final rupture with Gilbert in October 1893 the County Council had to make its own arrangements for the fountain. In November the height of the wall was reduced, but the Council refused to agree to the recommendation of its Improvements Committee that the wall should be altogether removed. (fn. 72) Experiments with the water supply and the jets were made throughout the winter, (fn. 73) and in April the Council accepted a second request from the Improvements Committee for the complete removal of the wall (fn. 74) . (fn. 5) In July the Council decided that, as the experiments had shown that whatever was done, water from the upper fountain frequently blew over the roadway, the water supply must be limited to the lower jets, and that in this limited fashion the fountain should play for ten hours daily at an annual cost of £234; the supply of drinking water was, however, to be constant. The Council also decided that the large stone block to which the inscription tablet had been fixed should be removed, and that the inscription should be re-cast in bronze slips and placed upon the faces of the fountain on the large chamfer above the lower basin. (fn. 75) In 1895 the shape of the pavement round the memorial was given an octagonal conformation. (fn. 76) In all the County Council spent £1558 upon the erection, adaptation and protection of a monument which had originally been offered by the Shaftesbury Memorial Committee as a gift. entries.outreach_draft:
Dear Westminster City Council,

We are writing on behalf of the production 'Piccadilly Circus' to request a location filming agreement for the use of footage filmed in Piccadilly Circus, London.

The material appears from approximately 0:00:00 to 0:01:00, for a duration of one minute. The footage prominently features Piccadilly Circus, including its iconic advertising hoardings, surrounding architecture, and the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain.

We seek rights for worldwide use, across all media, in perpetuity.

We have not established the current registered title for the Piccadilly Circus highway/public-space parcel or the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain. While evidence confirms council administration and historical municipal acceptance, the current land-title position remains unclear. Additionally, the exact statutory heritage status of the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain/Eros and the specific Piccadilly Circus parcel has not been confirmed from a definitive listing record. Westminster's published general conservation-area controls do not specifically identify Piccadilly Circus on the cited page. We would appreciate any guidance you can provide regarding the current ownership and heritage status of these elements.

Please confirm if you are able to grant this agreement, any associated fees, and any restrictions that may apply.

citations.title: Product Placement in Film: How It Works & How to Get It (2026) - Filmustage Blog
excerpts: Each sets a different price, level of control, and paperwork. ****- What you can land scales with your reach:**** indie/web/short-form → in-kind product and props that offset budget; mid-tier/streaming → mixed paid and trade; studio → paid integration plus co-promotion. ... **Classic product placement** is the prop on the table — historically supplied through _barter_ : a brand loans or gifts product (a car, a laptop, wardrobe) in exchange for screen time, with no fee changing hands. It adds realism and quietly offsets your budget. **Brand integration** is the paid version: the brand is named, used, and woven into the script as a plot-relevant element. It almost always involves [a cash fee, a media buy, or significant production support](https://hollywoodbranded.com/brand-integration-product-placement/?ref=blog.filmustage.com) — and it comes with guaranteed deliverables. **Sponsorship** is a fee to support the project with brand presence attached. **Co-promotion** is when the brand runs its _own_ advertising featuring your project — often the most valuable piece of all.

For a low-budget production, a handful of loaned vehicles, wardrobe pieces, and location dressing can take real money off the budget — and as your audience grows, paid deals open up too. ... excerpts: Hyundai Design and Technical Center in Irvine, Calif., and Sony Pictures collaborated on the design of the TUCSON “Beast” concept, which features a rugged exterior with fortified bumpers, tires and other outdoor-ready accoutrements that exhilarate the treasure-hunting escapade. “The Hyundai team has created a fun and global campaign that perfectly captures the adventurous tone of ‘Uncharted’ and further reinforces why they make such great partners,” said Jeffrey Godsick, EVP of Global Partnerships and Brand Management and Head of Location Based Entertainment at Sony Pictures Entertainment. While his car is being washed, Nathan relaxes at the car wash until the TUCSON is clean and ready for its next adventure. item.title: McDonald's
item.description: The McDonald's 'Golden Arches' logo and the slogan 'i'm lovin' it' appear as part of a cartoon advertisement on a central screen.
item.evidence: A cartoon advertisement featuring the McDonald's logo runs on a central panel of the display.

holders.name: McDonald’s Corporation
holders.territory: worldwide (subject to country-by-country confirmation and local-market clearance)
holders.contact: McDonald’s Global Legal Marketing/Intellectual Property legal team; the published brand guidance identifies Julie Arizzi, julie.arizzi@us.mcd.com, for trademark, slogan, and logo availability questions. Corporate Media Relations: press@us.mcd.com.
holders.notes: U.S. trademark records identify McDonald’s Corporation as owner of the “I’M LOVIN’ IT” registrations and the historical THE GOLDEN ARCHES filing. McDonald’s brand guidance calls for Global Brand Marketing and Global Marketing/IP legal approval for treatment of the Golden Arches. For a featured worldwide film depiction, obtain written trademark/brand approval rather than relying on incidental-use principles.

finding.public_domain_rationale: No. The requested material is being used as McDonald’s protected trademark and trade-dress assets, not as an unrestricted public-domain work. McDonald’s official terms identify its logos, slogans, trademarks, service marks, and trade dress as protected intellectual property, and its published media rules restrict logo use to specified editorial contexts. The age of the 1953 logo origin or 2003 slogan launch does not make the marks available for unrestricted commercial film use.
finding.territory_notes: McDonald’s Corporation is the identified U.S. proprietor, but trademark protection is territorial. Worldwide use requires confirmation of rights and approval in each relevant market; local McDonald’s counsel or market entities may need to participate. The requested worldwide, all-media, perpetual use should therefore be cleared expressly for every territory.
finding.licensing_precedent: Public sources document McDonald’s appearances and references in film and television, including The Founder (2016) and McDonald’s highlighted entertainment appearances in 2023. No publicly disclosed clearance agreement, licence term, or McDonald’s-specific fee was identified for those appearances. citations.title: McDonald’s History
excerpts: The Red and White The McDonald brothers insisted that their architect design an attention catching building that would highlight their Speedee Service System. Architect Stanley Meson design of the “Red and White” did not disappoint. Feeling that the roof line was a bit too flat Dick McDonald added arches to the building. This building design was first used in 1953 until it was replaced by the Mansard Roof design in the late 1960s. A sign maker incorporated yellow neon into them creating the “Golden Arches”. The oldest McDonald’s Red and White (opened in 1953) still operating today is in Downey, California. Early blueprints for signature McDonald’s Red and White restaurant with Speedee road sign.

finding.public_domain_rationale: The earliest documented St James Theatre branding work dates from 2011, with collateral including signage, posters, logos, screens, banners, and show branding. The U.S. Copyright Office states that post-1978 works generally last for the author's life plus 70 years, and works made for hire generally last 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation. Titles and short phrases alone are not protected by copyright, but sufficiently original logo artwork may be copyrighted and may also be protected as a trademark. Consequently, the modern graphic compilation is not safely public domain even though the individual show titles may not themselves be copyrightable.
finding.territory_notes: The exact printed panel is not identified, and no territorial split for that panel is documented. Worldwide, all-media, perpetual film use should be treated as requiring clearance of the underlying graphic artwork, any show logos or trademarks, the St James Theatre branding, and any photographs or illustrations. MTI states that it secured worldwide licensing rights for Billy Elliot The Musical, while Theatrical Rights Worldwide represents Jersey Boys for live-stage licensing and lists separate international offices. Those theatrical-performance mandates do not by themselves establish film/television reproduction rights.
finding.licensing_precedent: No documented film or television licence for this exact St James Theatre panel was identified. Public benchmarks are only indicative: one image-licensing schedule lists $25–$75 for video and film productions, while a film-artwork industry report states that many film budgets allow approximately $8,000–$25,000 for artwork. A comparable poster licence is described publicly as subject to a negotiated fee. Because this use is worldwide, all media, in perpetuity, and contains multiple identifiable theatre brands, the applicable fee could exceed a basic single-image rate.
unresolved: The exact printed panel, edition, date, and photographic source are unidentified; only the visible titles are known.
The original commissioning entity and copyright assignment for the St James Theatre compilation, signage, and collateral have not been established.

Dewynters established the initial St James Theatre logo, typography, and colour palette, while Katy Gunn developed collateral and signage through 2017; any assignment or licence from those creators to the theatre is unverified.

The current owner of the specific show poster or logo artwork for Billy Elliot, Jersey Boys, and Matilda has not been established. MTI and Theatrical Rights Worldwide are documented theatrical licensors, but their authority over film/television reproduction of historic advertising artwork is unconfirmed.
Any embedded photographs, illustrations, custom lettering, or third-party design elements in the panel have not been identified or separately cleared.
The exact first-publication date of this panel is unknown; 2011 is only the earliest documented date for the St James Theatre branding project.
No documented licence or fee for this exact panel in film or television was located; any fee estimate is therefore a market benchmark rather than a confirmed quote.

basis.reasoning: The St James Theatre branding and signage project is documented as modern work beginning in 2011. The Copyright Office term rules cover modern post-1978 works, while its guidance distinguishes uncopyrightable titles from potentially protected logo artwork. That makes a non-public-domain clearance position appropriate for the unidentified graphic panel.

excerpts: Patent & Trademark Office](https://www.uspto.gov/) at [TrademarkAssistanceCenter@uspto.gov](mailto: TrademarkAssistanceCenter@uspto.gov) or see [_Works Not Protected by Copyright_ (Circular 33) (PDF, 113 KB)](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf) for further information. **How do I copyright a name, title, slogan, or logo?** Copyright does not protect names, titles, slogans, or short phrases. Contact the [U.S. Patent & Trademark Office,](https://www.uspto.gov/) at [TrademarkAssistanceCenter@uspto.gov](mailto: TrademarkAssistanceCenter@uspto.gov) or see [_Works Not Protected by Copyright_ (Circular 33) (PDF, 113 KB)](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf) , for further information. citations.title: How Long Does Copyright Protection Last? (FAQ) | U.S. Copyright Office
excerpts: Home Help Frequently Asked Questions How Long Does Copyright Protection Last? How Long Does Copyright Protection Last? **How long does a copyright last?** The term of copyright for a particular work depends on several factors, including whether it has been published, and, if so, the date of first publication. As a general rule, for works created after January 1, 1978, copyright protection lasts for the life of the author plus an additional 70 years. For an anonymous work, a pseudonymous work, or a work made for hire, the copyright endures for a term of 95 years from the year of its first publication or a term of 120 years from the year of its creation, whichever expires first. For works first published prior to 1978, the term will vary depending on several factors.

citations.title: What Visual and Graphic Artists Should Know about Copyright | U.S. Copyright Office
excerpts: When it comes to copyright, creativity can be demonstrated in a variety of ways and reflects artistic choices like the subject matter, composition, depiction, and the use of the elements of design. Common symbols like smiley faces and hearts, as well as typography, are [ineligible for copyright protection](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf) . Very simple works, like stylized word logos or minimalist art, also might not be protected by copyright, although other legal protections, like [trademark protection](https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks) , may be available. Second, you should know that copyright protection exists from the moment an original work is “fixed” in a tangible medium. In the visual arts, for example, fixation occurs when you paint a picture or create digital art. Examples of visual artwork that can be protected by copyright include graphic art, paintings, sculptures, illustrations, architectural drawings, and more. Photography can also be protected by copyright. You don’t need to do anything else for your work to be protected by copyright, although you can register it with the U.S. Copyright Office for additional legal protections. Third, you should know that as the copyright owner, you have the right to make, sell, or otherwise distribute copies; adapt the work; and publicly display your work, including on the internet. If you want to use someone else’s work in these ways, you must get permission from the owner.

citations.title: What Visual and Graphic Artists Should Know about Copyright | U.S. Copyright Office
excerpts: When it comes to copyright, creativity can be demonstrated in a variety of ways and reflects artistic choices like the subject matter, composition, depiction, and the use of the elements of design. Common symbols like smiley faces and hearts, as well as typography, are [ineligible for copyright protection](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf) . Very simple works, like stylized word logos or minimalist art, also might not be protected by copyright, although other legal protections, like [trademark protection](https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks) , may be available. Second, you should know that copyright protection exists from the moment an original work is “fixed” in a tangible medium. In the visual arts, for example, fixation occurs when you paint a picture or create digital art. Examples of visual artwork that can be protected by copyright include graphic art, paintings, sculptures, illustrations, architectural drawings, and more. Photography can also be protected by copyright. You don’t need to do anything else for your work to be protected by copyright, although you can register it with the U.S. Copyright Office for additional legal protections. Third, you should know that as the copyright owner, you have the right to make, sell, or otherwise distribute copies; adapt the work; and publicly display your work, including on the internet. If you want to use someone else’s work in these ways, you must get permission from the owner.

finding.public_domain_rationale: The relevant footage appears to be from the short documentary Goodbye, Piccadilly, produced by the Rank Organisation in 1967. The U.S. Copyright Office states that works made for hire generally receive 95 years of protection from first publication; a 1967 corporate-produced film would therefore ordinarily remain protected through approximately the end of 2062. The available evidence does not establish a public-domain exception, a lapsed U.S. copyright, or a complete rights chain, so the footage should not be treated as public domain.
finding.territory_notes: The requested clearance is worldwide, all media, in perpetuity. The U.S. registration identifies GAP (APPAREL), LLC as proprietor of a GAP logo registration, while Gap Inc.'s terms state that GAP marks are owned by Gap Inc. and/or its subsidiaries. Non-U.S. trademark ownership, local franchise rights, and any territory-specific film/television approval authority must be confirmed separately. Gap's public policy does not offer a worldwide entertainment-clearance route and states that it does not grant permission for use or modification of its trademarks.
finding.licensing_precedent: No publicly documented prior film or television licence, approval, or reported fee for this specific GAP storefront/logo use was located. Gap's published permission policy says it does not grant permission to use or modify its trademarks, logos, images, advertising, or similar materials and will not respond to those requests; this is a general policy, not an entertainment-specific approval precedent.

excerpts: **15A** For works made for hire and anonymous and pseudonymous works, the duration of copyright is 95 years from first publication or 120 years from creation, whichever is shorter (unless the author’s identity is later revealed in Copyright Office records, in which case the term becomes the author’s life plus 70 years). For more information about works made for hire, see _Works Made for Hire_ ( **Circular 30** ). For details about pseudonymous works, see _Pseudonyms (_ **Circular 32** ). ... The duration of copyright in these works is generally computed the same way as for works created on or after January 1, 1978: life plus 70 years or 95 or 120 years, depending on the nature of authorship. However, all works in this category are guaranteed at least 25 years of statutory protection. ...

finding.public_domain_rationale: The Mastercard interlocking-circle design and word mark are trademarks, not copyright works whose protection has expired. Mastercard’s official Brand Center describes the interlocking red and yellow circles as the Mastercard Symbol and identifies Mastercard International Incorporated in the trademark attribution language. It also states that the materials are protected by trademark law and that commercial use of Mastercard trademarks requires prior written permission. Mastercard’s official history dates adoption of the two-circle Master Charge brand mark to 1968; that age does not place the trademark in the public domain.
finding.territory_notes: Mastercard International Incorporated is identified as the proprietor of the relevant U.S. marks. The requested license is worldwide, so clearance should be confirmed for non-U.S. territories and any territory-specific Mastercard affiliate or trademark owner. Mastercard’s public Brand Center provides global branding guidance but does not publish a territory-by-territory entertainment-clearance schedule.
finding.licensing_precedent: No publicly documented film or television license, prior entertainment clearance, or reported fee for the Mastercard name or interlocking-circle logo was located. Public materials document Mastercard sponsorship and marketing activity, but not a standardized entertainment licensing precedent or fee.
unresolved: Mastercard’s public materials do not expressly identify a dedicated film-and-television licensing department or confirm that ask.brand.manager@mastercard.com is authorized to approve worldwide entertainment depictions.

The public U.S. trademark list and registrations do not establish ownership of every non-U.S. registration covering the Mastercard word mark and interlocking-circle symbol; worldwide title should be confirmed with Mastercard’s legal or brand team.

The production’s depiction is a sponsored-event graphic in the background, but no written sponsorship, event-owner, or production release was provided confirming the right to reproduce the specific West End Live artwork. The event organizer or artwork owner may require a separate clearance.

basis.reasoning: The Brand Center expressly states that the materials are protected by U.S. and foreign trademark laws and that reproduction beyond limited purposes requires written permission. The Terms of Use separately state that commercial use of a Mastercard trademark requires prior written permission. Those statements directly support that the mark is not public-domain material.

citations.title: Brand History | Mastercard US
excerpts: As the consumer and commerce landscape continues to evolve, the Mastercard Symbol is a modern and flexible brand design optimized to work seamlessly across the digital landscape. Changes in the Mastercard Brand Mark over time reflect our increasingly global reach. In the early years of our brand, lnterbank was represented by the “i” symbol—a straightforward means of identifying participating members of the Interbank Card Association. Here’s how it came about: 1967 Seventeen bankers meet in Buffalo, New York to form a federation for the reciprocal acceptance of their credit cards. Interbankard adopts the “i” symbol as its mark. The federation becomes formally chartered in 1967—The Interbank Card Association (ICA). 1968 The Master Charge name and graphics are adopted to provide stronger brand identification. The new brand mark features the Master Charge name centered between two interlocking circles of red and ocher. The “i” symbol is retained in a smaller size at the bottom right corner for purposes of continuity. 1979 Master Charge becomes MasterCard. The “i” symbol is then retired in 1980.

finding.public_domain_rationale: The material is a trademark/logo rather than a conventional copyrighted work. The available UK record identifies a registered Boots figurative mark filed and registered in 1984, while Boots' legal notice says that website content confers no licence or right under the Company's trademarks. No evidence establishes that the depicted logo is free of copyright in the United States, and trademark protection remains territorial; therefore a definitive US public-domain determination is not supported.
finding.territory_notes: There is no single worldwide Boots trademark right. The Boots Company PLC is identified as proprietor of the relevant UK Boots registration and as an owner of trademark records in both USPTO and EUIPO datasets, but the exact blue-oval storefront mark and any assignments or licences must be checked separately in each territory. For the requested worldwide, all-media, perpetual use, obtain express written approval covering the United Kingdom, United States, European Union and every other intended territory. Boots UK Limited is the UK operating company and the practical media contact, but it is not identified in the available records as the registered proprietor of the mark.
finding.licensing_precedent: No Boots-specific film or television trademark licence, approval, or fee is publicly documented in the located material. A publicly indexed student letter shows a request to film a short scene inside a Boots store, but it does not document whether permission was granted or any payment.
unresolved: The cited UK registration UK00001216763 is a registered Boots figurative mark filed in 1984, but the available record does not establish that it is the exact blue oval storefront logo or identify the relevant retail-services registration for this shot.
The current status of the publicly listed Group Intellectual Property contact for The Boots Company PLC has not been independently confirmed; the published contact record is dated 2016.

finding.public_domain_rationale: The earliest documented St James Theatre branding work dates from 2011, with collateral including signage, posters, logos, screens, banners, and show branding. The U.S. Copyright Office states that post-1978 works generally last for the author's life plus 70 years, and works made for hire generally last 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation. Titles and short phrases alone are not protected by copyright, but sufficiently original logo artwork may be copyrighted and may also be protected as a trademark. Consequently, the modern graphic compilation is not safely public domain even though the individual show titles may not themselves be copyrightable.
finding.territory_notes: The exact printed panel is not identified, and no territorial split for that panel is documented. Worldwide, all-media, perpetual film use should be treated as requiring clearance of the underlying graphic artwork, any show logos or trademarks, the St James Theatre branding, and any photographs or illustrations. MTI states that it secured worldwide licensing rights for Billy Elliot The Musical, while Theatrical Rights Worldwide represents Jersey Boys for live-stage licensing and lists separate international offices. Those theatrical-performance mandates do not by themselves establish film/television reproduction rights.
finding.licensing_precedent: No documented film or television licence for this exact St James Theatre panel was identified. Public benchmarks are only indicative: one image-licensing schedule lists $25–$75 for video and film productions, while a film-artwork industry report states that many film budgets allow approximately $8,000–$25,000 for artwork. A comparable poster licence is described publicly as subject to a negotiated fee. Because this use is worldwide, all media, in perpetuity, and contains multiple identifiable theatre brands, the applicable fee could exceed a basic single-image rate.
unresolved: The exact printed panel, edition, date, and photographic source are unidentified; only the visible titles are known.
The original commissioning entity and copyright assignment for the St James Theatre compilation, signage, and collateral have not been established.

Dewynters established the initial St James Theatre logo, typography, and colour palette, while Katy Gunn developed collateral and signage through 2017; any assignment or licence from those creators to the theatre is unverified.

The current owner of the specific show poster or logo artwork for Billy Elliot, Jersey Boys, and Matilda has not been established. MTI and Theatrical Rights Worldwide are documented theatrical licensors, but their authority over film/television reproduction of historic advertising artwork is unconfirmed.
Any embedded photographs, illustrations, custom lettering, or third-party design elements in the panel have not been identified or separately cleared.
The exact first-publication date of this panel is unknown; 2011 is only the earliest documented date for the St James Theatre branding project.
No documented licence or fee for this exact panel in film or television was located; any fee estimate is therefore a market benchmark rather than a confirmed quote.

You may express your ideas in writing or drawings and claim copyright in your description, but be aware that copyright will not protect the idea itself as revealed in your written or artistic work. **Does my work have to be published to be protected?** Publication is not necessary for copyright protection. citations.title: Departure 2093 - My passion
excerpts: Five visions of **future flying** Kauko Helavuo, Studio Kauko Helavuo My passion – the future of flying The designer's own account of his method, and the specification list underneath every drawing. Kauko Helavuo drew the five concept aircraft that became the most reproduced part of this project. His essay explains where they came from, and it is disarmingly unmethodical about it. ... His definition of the future > “For me, the definition of the word future is best described as inspirational and challenging. > The future creates positive energy and it gives us the freedom to enjoy the world of knowledge and > imagination. Furthermore, the future is always a beginning of something new.”Kauko Helavuo, Studio Kauko Helavuo That is a designer’s statement, not a forecaster’s, and the essay does not pretend otherwise.
